Have you ever paid someone to buy something from you? Let’s say you want to sell your car. Would you pay the buyer to take the car from you?
Well, something like that happened in the crude oil market during the Covid pandemic in 2020. In April 2020, the WTI crude oil contract for May 2020 had dropped to -$37.63 per barrel.
Read it again. That’s negative $37.63. This means you could basically buy crude oil and not pay for it; instead, you would be paid for it.
How did that happen?
See, the lockdowns from Covid had largely shut down industries and transportation. People could not travel. So, the demand for oil had suddenly dropped.
And crude oil is traded in the futures market. So when many countries started imposing lockdowns.the oil futures contracts that were trading around $60-$65 a barrel in January 2020 fell to around $20-$25 in March 2020,
Let’s say you were a trader observing this massive 60% plus fall in oil prices. You thought to yourself, it doesn’t feel like oil prices could go down any further. So you bought a few May 2020 crude oil contracts at around $20 per barrel.
You were hoping that crude prices would revive and you would sell the contracts for a profit.
But this is how reality unfolded.
Oil demand continued to fall. However, oil-producing countries were still hopeful of a revival and wanted to be prepared for it. So, they continued to produce and increase the oil supply in the market. As a result of this, oil prices also continued to fall.
Remember that you, as a trader, were looking to sell the crude oil contracts at a profit.
When you buy a crude futures contract, you can exit the position in two ways.
First, sell the contract before expiry and square off your position.
Second, hold it until expiry and take delivery of the oil barrels. Yes, you will have to take physical delivery.
As the contract expiry approached closer, you got scared.
The first option of selling the contract before expiry was not working. There were no buyers.
There was no way you could take the second option. You are just a trader in the global financial markets sitting in front of your screen. You are not into the oil business. You have no warehouses, where would you take the delivery?
Even the traders who were into the oil business and could take physical delivery had been running out of storage space. Many started maintaining floating warehouses by storing the crude oil in tankers. Even they had contracts for which they did not have enough space to take delivery.
This created a panic among those who had bought the crude futures contracts. When they couldn’t sell it for even zero dollars, they started selling at negative prices. Basically, they were paying the buyers to take physical crude oil deliveries that they could not take.
Globally, no instrument or commodity in any market had ever before seen prices go to negative.
Actually, up until this point, there were no systems—a trader’s front end, order management, and risk management—designed to manage negative prices, so this also created some commotion.
Sometimes things that have never happened but are theoretically possible can happen in the most unexpected ways and for the most unexpected reasons.
We can prepare for known risks but not so much for unknown risks. And what we can control is how much risk we take in our investment or trading decisions.
It is better to be aware of how much risk or losses you can stomach and accordingly size your bets.

In 1935, Austrian physicist Erwin Schrödinger proposed a thought experiment . It involved putting a cat inside a sealed box. And alongside it would be a radioactive element that had a random chance of being released.
He claimed that in such a situation, you don’t know if the cat is actually dead or alive until you open the box. So, until you open the box and look, the cat exists in both states simultaneously — alive and dead.
It sounds absurd.
But since it was a thought experiment for quantum mechanics, I won’t get into the details. Just that for some weird reason this “Schrödinger’s Cat” became hugely popular. People began to use it to describe any situation where they are stuck in suspense. For example: “until I check my bank account, I am both rich and broke”.
But hold on…why are we talking about Schrödinger and his cat now?
Well, because right now, if you opened a box of the world economy, you’d find that cat staring back at you.
I’ll explain.
And let’s talk about the US since it’s the world’s biggest economy.
US real GDP grew by 2.7% in the first quarter of 2026 (that’s Jan-March). That might not seem like anything to write home about but it’s actually pretty good for a market like America. And for anyone who tracks the US, just that headline number would tell you the economy is doing fairly well.
But let’s break that down a bit.
If you see what contributed to the GDP, you’ll find that 43% of it is because of AI-related capital expenditure — in software, data centre construction etc.
Source: Jefferies
And If you set aside the AI investments that have been propping up the economy over the past year or so, some analysts from Deutsche Bank say the US would have fallen into a recession .
Alive and dead.
That’s the state of economic growth.
Now let’s talk about jobs.
The US has something called the non-farm payrolls . This accounts for nearly 80% of workers in the country and excludes farm employees, domestic help, and the self-employed. It’s the number to track to understand whether the country is adding jobs and growing or not.
And the latest number surprised everyone. In a good way. Analysts expected around 85,000 new jobs to be added. But the numbers came in at 172,000 for May.
Way better.
But, strip that down and you’ll see something a bit concerning. 70,000 of those new jobs were in the hospitality segment. And that’s only because of the football world cup. The jobs are probably not going to be permanent. And apart from this, education, and healthcare, only 10,000 other jobs were created in other sectors.
That concentration might be a problem. ING’s report noted , “While this is a very good report at the headline level, the lack of breadth to the job creation story remains an important theme.”
Alive and dead.
Sort of.
Also, the thing with a booming AI industry is that it is capital intensive but not labour intensive. So if an economy is looking to add jobs and reduce unemployment, it probably won’t help with that. In fact, it’s not really great for the college-educated crowd either.
And while we cannot just blame AI, just look at this chart from the New York Federal Reserve which shows the unemployment rates. You can see it clearly inching upwards, faster for college graduates when compared to all workers.
Source: NY Fed
And it’s not just unemployment but even underemployment that has been on the rise for this cohort. Underemployment is when you do a job that you’re overqualified for — like flipping burgers after getting a college degree.
In the US, the underemployment rate for recent college graduates is at 41.5% . It’s the highest level since the pandemic.
Alive and dead.
Even the stock market is like Schrödinger’s cat.
The S&P 500 is made up of 500 of the biggest stocks in the US and it is meant to be a fairly broad representation of 11 different industries that drive the economy.
But if you dissect what’s going on in the index, you’ll find something quite interesting.
UBS research has picked 45 stocks out of the 500 that it believes are leading the charge in AI. And the returns from just these stocks are nearly 60% this year alone.
Strip those out, look at the rest of the 455 stocks, and the index is flat. Pretty much 0% returns.
Source: The Guardian
The stock market is….
…alive and dead.
But if you set all this complex economic stuff aside and want to explain to your 5-year kid what a Schrödinger’s economy really looks like, you just need to talk about McDonald’s . Yup, the fast food chain has declared that while traffic from higher-income customers has jumped by double digits, traffic from lower-income customers has actually declined.
Alive and dead.
And that’s why everyone’s confused — policymakers, citizens, everyone.
You see, for most of 2025 and into 2026, the US Federal Reserve has been caught between two mandates that are pointing in opposite directions. On one side inflation remains stubbornly above its 2% target; it’s at over 4% now. On the other hand, the job market is softening, growth is showing a clear reliance only on AI, and warnings of recession have been sounded.
The Fed’s choice, in a normal world, is simple. Inflation too high? Raise rates. Economy slowing? Cut rates. But what do you do when both are true simultaneously?
If it cuts rates to help the slowing economy, it risks reigniting inflation — which already burned millions of ordinary Americans for three years. If it holds rates high to fight inflation, it risks tipping a fragile economy into recession — which would hurt those same ordinary Americans even more.
The contradictory signals have left the Fed confused. At their December 2025 meeting on interest rates, three of the twelve voting members openly dissented — the highest level of internal disagreement since 2019 — while the Fed’s own internal projections showed a more dispersed range of forecasts about the future path of rates than at any recent meeting.
When even the committee itself can’t agree on what to do, that tells you something about the state of the data it’s reading.
And there’s a deeper problem with a Schrödinger economy too — It’s that bad policy tends to follow bad data.
When the headline numbers look okay, there is enormous political pressure to say the economy is fine and to resist calls for intervention because the aggregate data doesn’t justify it.
But if the aggregate data is obscuring a K-shaped, Schrödinger reality underneath, then “don’t intervene because GDP looks good” could make things worse.
And that is a problem that policymakers are dealing with.
Now that we’ve talked about the US, do you think India is also a Schrödinger’s economy currently? Tell us in the comments.

When you buy a computer or a laptop, in all likelihood, you will also buy a Microsoft Office pack with it. That Office pack lets you use Microsoft Word, Excel, or PowerPoint. Earlier, it was a one-time purchase. You could use it for years. But now you also have the pay-per-year model, or a subscription model. And Microsoft, in fact, wants you to buy this subscription version.
In this newsletter, we’ll try and understand Microsoft’s motivation behind switching its pricing from a one-time purchase to a subscription model.
Microsoft launched its first-ever Office Suite with Word, Excel, and PowerPoint back in 1989-1990. You would buy the suite once, often as a box of CDs or a one-time download, and use it for years. Microsoft would launch new versions every three years or so. But as a customer, you could continue using the older versions. This went on for nearly two decades before a dramatic change.
In 2013, Microsoft introduced Office 365, a subscription-based version of Office. Essentially, it was steering away from selling a static product and reinventing it “as a consumer cloud service”. Instead of paying, say, Rs 10,000 upfront for Office 2024 and keeping that same version indefinitely, customers could now pay about Rs 7000 per year for Office 365. It would give access to all that the static version would offer, but on five devices, plus extras like online storage and continuous new feature upgrades.
Office 365 blew up that three-year cycle. The subscription model let Office evolve continuously rather than in big jumps every few years. This ensured users always have the latest features without having to manually purchase an upgrade or reinstall software.
It was also a response to the changing times. The early 2010s saw the rise of cloud computing and software-as-a-service. Companies like Google were offering Google Docs and other Office apps essentially for free. Other rivals were moving to more agile development cycles.
Microsoft never publicly admitted that Google triggered a switch in its business model. But it was only natural for Microsoft to introduce a similar subscription version like Google. Microsoft’s move was partly defensive – to ensure Office remained relevant in a cloud-connected world – and partly an offensive play to leverage its huge user base into a cloud service.
The pivot to subscriptions was also driven by solid business reasoning. Instead of seeing a spike in sales whenever a new Office version launched and then a lull as sales tailed off, a subscription model would generate recurring income every month or year. Investors and executives love predictable revenue — it’s easier to forecast and companies with high subscription revenues also enjoy higher valuations.
Beyond the recurring revenue, customer lifetime value tends to increase under subscriptions. Subscriptions increase stickiness. Moreover, if a customer is accustomed to using Microsoft’s Office suite, they might find it difficult to switch to Office substitutes, such as those offered by Google and others. So, they might just continue to pay for Microsoft Office.
Microsoft clearly recognized this “annuity” value. Such a model also changes the relationship with the customer — instead of a one-and-done transaction, Microsoft can now have an ongoing engagement with Office 365 users, giving it more opportunities to upsell new features.
Stickiness is even higher among business customers. Businesses find it extremely challenging to switch their existing Office suite. It involves several weeks, if not months, of communication, training, handholding, and follow-up to get all employees comfortable with a new Office Suite. And while such a switch happens, the operations could slow down, employee responsiveness might get delayed, and productivity hampered. So, if a business buys Microsoft’s Office suite, most likely it will stick with Microsoft for a very long time.
This is also a drawback, though. If a customer is already using, say, Google Workspace, it becomes that much more difficult to convince them to switch to Microsoft.
And customer stickiness or not, such a switch in pricing is often seen as a gamble. Existing customers may have felt that Microsoft had found a way to milk their pockets.
But Microsoft had not abandoned its one-time-purchase offering. If you want, you can still make that one-time purchase and not pay annual subscriptions. However, you might feel a differential treatment being meted out to you because you did not choose to subscribe. Indeed, Microsoft heavily promotes the subscription versions.
So did the bet pay off?
Early signs indicated yes. Within just over three months of its debut, Office 365 Home Premium hit over one million subscribers. For comparison, that adoption outpaced some other big subscription launches; it took Adobe about seven months to reach a million subscribers after it shifted Photoshop and its creative suite to the cloud. Microsoft even touted that the 2013 release of Office was the “best-selling Office edition yet,” with more than one copy being sold every second at one point.
Microsoft’s stock price, which had remained practically flat for almost 12 years after the dot-com bubble, actually started rallying 2013 onwards.
Basically, the market was validating Microsoft’s new strategy. Fast forward to today, and subscriptions have clearly become the norm for Office. It has been renamed to Microsoft 365, signalling a broader, cloud-focused offering beyond just the core Office apps.
As of 2024, Microsoft 365 had over 400 million users. That massive subscriber base translates into a huge, reliable revenue stream.
You know one serious benefit of a subscription model?
The scope of piracy is low.
Software piracy was a major issue. Microsoft Office was widely pirated. Even Adobe estimated over 40% piracy rates for its perpetually licensed software in some markets. A subscription tied to cloud services and frequent updates can mitigate piracy. It is harder to pirate something that requires online account checks and is constantly changing. It also ensures more users are on the latest version rather than a mishmash of old versions. This uniformity can lower support costs and security risks since fewer customers are stuck on outdated, unsupported software.
As far as customers are concerned, the subscription model is better suited in two ways.
One, they get new updates as and when they are released,
And two, they can use Microsoft Office on multiple devices
However, costs might be a bit too high for them. Of course, the upfront cost goes down, but the customer has to bear a recurring cost every year. And it might even grow with inflation.
Then there is subscription fatigue. How many subscriptions can one really handle?
Gym subscriptions, Netflix, insurance premiums, Cloud storage, even meal kits. And of course, Microsoft Office. All those recurring charges add up, and consume a substantial portion of one’s income. The psychological effect of too many subscriptions can turn people off, and a product that might have been fine as a one-time purchase could lose customers if they don’t want yet another ongoing bill.
Microsoft, however, did not lose customers.
In fact, Microsoft’s shift with Office is part of a much broader trend in the software industry. Many software companies that once sold boxed software have pivoted to subscriptions to stay competitive and meet investor expectations. One of the most cited examples is Adobe, the maker of Photoshop and other creative tools.
Companies like Oracle and SAP that traditionally sold expensive on-premise licenses are now pushing cloud subscription versions of their software. Even smaller software startups today almost all start with a Software-as-a-Service subscription model by default – it’s just how software is commonly delivered now.
Of course, it is not cast in stone. Businesses have designed different pricing models now.
Some businesses highlight their one-time purchase model as a selling point to differentiate from subscription-heavy competitors.
Some others offer both models: a subscription for those who prefer smaller payments and constant updates, and a one-time purchase of a perpetual license for those who want full ownership. Microsoft is a case in point.
Then there are hybrid approaches: some software subscriptions allow you to keep using the last version you downloaded, even if you stop your subscription.
These nuances show that businesses are experimenting to find the sweet spot that customers accept.
Interestingly, moving to a subscription model is far more common than moving back to one-time sales, but there are examples of the latter in a roundabout way. In the gaming industry, for instance, many online games used to require monthly subscriptions to play, like the famous World of Warcraft. Over time, many of those shifted to free-to-play or one-time purchase models with optional microtransactions, because players showed resistance to too many subscriptions.
So, while the tide is toward subscriptions, savvy companies have listened to their users and sometimes course-corrected if a pure-subscription strategy wasn’t feasible for their customers.

The US Central Bank has a new chairperson — Kevin Warsh. And he has a different agenda. He wants to talk as little as possible.
I’ll explain.
On 17th June, the US Federal Reserve’s Open Market Committee (FOMC)— the folks in charge of setting interest rates — had just wrapped up their 2-day long discussion and Warsh had to tell the world what they’d all decided.
They kept interest rates on hold (at 3.50% to 3.75% ) but that wasn’t the interesting part.
Rather, what I want to tell you is that the FOMC’s post-meeting statement was just 131 words , down from 341 words in April. Warsh then refused to answer questions around “What would the Fed do if data said x or y.” And finally, when it came time to release the popular “dot plot” — which anonymously tracks what each Fed official thinks about future interest rates — there were 18 dots on it instead of 19.
Kevin Warsh’s dot was missing. On purpose.
Source: US Federal Reserve
Kevin Warsh thinks central bankers (like the US Fed) talk too much. And he wants to change that.
He thinks the speeches, the forward guidance, the dot plot, the press conferences after literally every single meeting has made markets addicted to the Fed’s voice instead of letting prices do the talking. His take is that ,
“Financial market prices are probably the most important source of information to guide central bankers. But when all the financial markets are doing is reflecting back what we’ve said, then we’re taking the most important source of information, and we’re being blind to it.”
Because central bankers have so much power, investors spend all their time trying to guess exactly what the central bank will do next. Instead of pricing stocks and bonds based on the real economy, the market starts pricing them purely based on what the central bank said it was going to do.
If the market stops looking at the real world and only looks at the central bank, the feedback loop breaks.
And when the central bank looks at the market for guidance, they aren’t looking at the real economy anymore. They are just looking into a mirror.
Put simply, Warsh wants the markets to reflect the information out there.And he wants the Fed to react to what the market tells them.
So he’s trying to go quiet.
So why does this matter to us?
After all, we in India have nothing to do with the Fed.
Because this isn’t really a story about Kevin Warsh. It’s a story about why every central bank across the world has increasingly built a system where there’s more talking, not less.
Hear me out.
What’s a central banker’s job?
You might say. “To manage inflation.”
And it is.
They call it price stability. And they manage inflation with the help of their “monetary” powers. Which means they raise interest rates when inflation is high and hope it dissuades people from borrowing money and spending. Less demand for goods and services will thus lower inflation. And it works in reverse too. They cut interest rates when they want to spur the economy.
But, over decades, central bankers developed one specific belief. That if people expect low, stable inflation, they’ll act in ways that make inflation low and stable. Workers won’t demand huge raises to keep up with prices they think are coming. Businesses won’t jack up prices preemptively. If everyone just believes inflation will be 2% (that’s what countries like the US have targeted), inflation tends to land near 2%.
This is called: anchoring inflation expectations.
And today, the idea of anchoring leading to inflation control is close to gospel truth in the central banking circles. It’s because of this innate belief that expectations of inflation can be influenced that central bankers have gone all out in their communication strategies.
The Bank of Canada ran a public campaign called “Let’s Talk Inflation.” It’s why the European Central Bank built pages on its own website called “The ECB and You” to explain their decision making process. And it’s why you’ll find central bankers showing up on podcasts, on Instagram, even using reggae songs to get the message. That’s in Jamaica , of course!.
And the RBI hasn’t sat this one out either. Since adopting inflation targeting in 2016, India’s central bank publishes minutes ( pdf ) two weeks after every policy meeting, a monetary policy report every six months explaining where inflation is headed, and a governor’s press conference after every rate decision.
The explicit goal is anchoring the public’s inflation expectations.
In other words: talking is the policy tool and not just a side effect of policy.
The talking itself is supposed to move inflation.
And central banks have taken up the task because if you don’t show up and explain yourself clearly, somebody else will explain you — badly, or incorrectly. In fact, a 2019 NBER paper ( pdf ) found that messages coming straight from the central bank were around twice as persuasive at shaping people’s inflation expectations as the same message summarised secondhand through a news article.
So, if you want people’s expectations anchored, apparently, you have to be the one doing the anchoring. Outsourcing it to halves the effect.
But of course, as with everything in economics, not everyone agrees that there’s a real cause-and-effect at play here. And in 2021, a Fed staff economist named Jeremy Rudd published an internal paper ( pdf ) that didn’t pull any punches in calling this out. He opened with this:
“Mainstream economics is replete with ideas that ‘everyone knows’ to be true, but that are actually arrant nonsense.”
And one of the ideas he was talking about was anchoring. He called central bank dependence on communication as “an important policy goal or instrument” “unnecessary and unsound.”
His words, not mine.
His case is that the evidence isn’t strong enough to indicate that anchoring actually helps. And his alternative explanation was that inflation gets anchored when it’s not on anyone’s “radar screens”. Simply because nobody’s paying close attention to it in the first place — and constantly drawing attention to it might actually be counterproductive.
So who’s actually right?
It’s probably somewhere in between, honestly.
It would be a stretch to say central bank communication does nothing. The NBER finding that direct communication is twice as persuasive as secondhand reporting suggests people genuinely do update their beliefs based on what a central bank says.
And there’s a simpler, harder-to-dismiss reason central banks talk. It’s to do with accountability. An unelected (mostly) committee that controls interest rates for an entire economy probably does owe the public some explanation for what it’s doing and why — separate from whether that explanation actually bends the inflation numbers.
Which brings us back to Kevin Warsh, standing at that podium, trying to talk less.
He’s not wrong that there’s a lot of noise. But while he might choose to stay quiet, the other people on the Fed’s rate-setting committee are still free to say whatever they want, whenever they want. Regional Fed presidents give speeches. They do interviews. So Warsh can be quiet. But the Fed, as an institution, cannot.
And that’s because that’s the belief. A belief that central banks have to do anything at their disposal to meet their primary objective — inflation management. And if communicating to the public is one lever they can tap into, they will.
That’s just the way it is.

There’s a glaring contradiction in India today.
The Nifty 50 — India’s benchmark stock market index — is down roughly 10% this year. Meanwhile, India’s GDP has grown 7.7% in FY26.
So, which one is lying?
The textbook answer is that neither is a lie. You’ve heard experts say, “the stock market is not the economy,” right?
Well, you could say that is what is at play here. A stock market correction can happen for a hundred reasons that have nothing to do with how factories, farms, and offices are actually doing.
And while that might sound comforting, there might be cause for worry too.
Because of something called the t heory of reflexivity which, in essence, tells us the stock market can be the economy.
So let me step back and break it down.
In 1987, a young George Soros (yes, the very man associated with a lot of conspiracy theories these days) published a book titled The Alchemy of Finance. He was a hedge fund trader. He’d studied at the London School of Economics. But he was a philosopher at heart.
Without getting into too many details, Soros finished his course at LSE a year early but had to stick around to actually get the degree. So he spent his time under the tutelage of a philosopher Karl Popper whose writings began to influence Soros in a big way. In economics, Soros was learning about assumptions around perfect competition. On the other hand, Popper’s work spoke about imperfect understanding of the world around us, including scientific laws.
So The Alchemy of Finance was Soros’ attempt to explain his philosophical approach to financial markets. He replaced the standard assumptions of rational expectations and efficient markets with his own principles — of fallibility and something he called reflexivity.
This is how he explains fallibility:
…in situations that have thinking participants, the participants’ views of the world never perfectly correspond to the actual state of affairs. People can gain knowledge of individual facts, but when it comes to formulating theories or forming an overall view, their perspective is bound to be either biased or inconsistent or both.
Or in simpler terms, because the world is extremely complex, we don’t have the capacity to fully understand it. And so, we resort to generalizations in an attempt to simplify things.
Reflexivity on the other hand builds on this:
…these distorted views can influence the situation to which they relate because false views lead to inappropriate actions.
The one-line version is this: fallibility explains why the gap between belief and reality exists in the first place; reflexivity explains what happens once people start acting on that gap.
From a market perspective,
…if investors believe that markets are efficient then that belief will change the way they invest, which in turn will change the nature of the markets in which they are participating (though not necessarily making them more efficient).
It’s a thinking-reality feedback loop.
Most of the time, this loop is small and harmless. Stock falls a bit, nobody cares, life moves on. But sometimes the loop finds something to grip onto. And it starts to feed itself.
Which brings us back to that contradiction. Markets are falling, GDP is rising. Could this be one of the moments where the loop is just getting started?
Okay, so on its own, the correction is just noise. Markets correct, and they have for as long as there have been markets. Crude oil near $80-$90 a barrel, a weak rupee, a geopolitical shock from the US-Iran-Israel conflict. Simple — there’s no need to bring fallibility and reflexivity into this.
Except, India’s stock market has changed dramatically in the past 5-6 years. People are participating in a big way. I mean, look at some of these numbers from the Economic Survey ( pdf ):
The share of individual investors increased from ~11 per cent in FY14 to 14.3 per cent in FY19, and further to 18.8 per cent by September 2025.
The share of equity and mutual funds in annual household financial savings increased from ~2 per cent in FY12 to over 15.2 per cent in FY25.
…steady rise in SIP contributions, with average monthly SIP flows increasing seven times from under ₹4,000 crore in FY17 to over Rs 28,000 crore in FY26 (April-November).
Between April 2020 to September 2025, household equity wealth is estimated to have increased by about ₹53 lakh crore, underscoring the role of sustained participation in driving long-term wealth creation in equity markets.
All of a sudden, the equity markets are housing a meaningfully large chunk of the Indian household balance sheet that didn’t exist five years ago.
Source: Economic Survey
But there’s a risk.
It’s a risk that the Economic Survey flagged as well before this correction began. It warned that a sharp fall in equities could dent the sentiment and spending of retail investors directly — and that the effect could “cascade,” given how many of these investors are young, newly arrived in the market, and have never actually lived through a real downturn.
Translation: a chunk of India’s spending power is now wired to the Sensex or Nifty ticking up or down.
That’s the gripping point for the loop.
Look at SIP behaviour — the most disciplined, least emotional corner of Indian retail investing, the one everybody points to as proof that Indians have finally learned to invest for the long term, untouched by panic.
In March 2026, the SIP stoppage ratio — the number of SIPs discontinued versus newly started — crossed 100%. This means more SIPs were being shut than opened.
To be fair, some of that “stoppage” is just SIPs naturally finishing their tenure. It isn’t a clean signal of fear.
But it isn’t nothing either. Look at this chart of the past SIP stoppage ratios. It’s very rarely this high.
Source: Moneycontrol
Which means, the most “set it and forget it” form of investing in India is suddenly seeing more exits than entries, in the very moment a correction is underway.
If perception is shifting even in SIP behaviour, the next domino is consumption. Someone who watches their portfolio shrink doesn’t necessarily sell their house, but they might put off buying the new phone, delay the car upgrade, skip the vacation, postpone the home renovation.
Multiply that hesitation across the millions of active traders and crores of SIP holders and you don’t need anyone to be irrational. You just need enough people to feel a little less rich than they did a few weeks ago.
But hold on…isn’t that just the wealth effect at play?
So, I’ve written about the wealth effect before ( here ) and it sounds like the same thing at first. It says that when stock prices fall, households feel poorer, and they spend less.
But that is one-directional.
Reflexivity makes a stronger and different claim that the belief itself , once it starts shaping behavior, changes the fundamentals that the belief was supposedly just tracking. And then the changed fundamentals feed back into the belief, in a loop.
If a stock market correction hits, reflexivity shows that the damage to investor and executive confidence forces real-world changes that validate the market’s pessimism. For example,
As stock prices plummet, banks and bond markets grow nervous. They tighten lending standards or raise interest rates. Companies that rely on rolling over debt suddenly find it expensive or impossible to do so, threatening their solvency. That’s a credit freeze.
Corporate executives watch their stock prices tank. To protect their balance sheets and satisfy shareholders, they cancel capital expenditure projects, freeze hiring, or start layoffs. That’s corporate austerity.
Because companies are cutting spending and laying off workers, unemployment rises and economic growth slows. The market correction created the economic downturn that justified the lower stock prices in the first place. That’s the self-fulfilling prophecy.
In short, Soros’ reflexivity loop says that: consumption softens, corporate earnings reflect that softness, and the market reads weaker earnings as confirmation that the correction was justified all along — which pushes the market down further — which makes people feel poorer again.
The fall causes the slowdown. The slowdown justifies the fall.
Fallibility and reflexivity.
Now, is this actually happening in India? Honestly, it’s too early to say.
A few weeks of selling by foreign investors and a geopolitical shock don’t automatically tip into a consumption slowdown. SIP inflows, even with the higher stoppage ratio, still are at record highs — ₹32,000 crores. People are still putting money in even as some pull money out. And there’s a reasonable counterargument that India’s correction so far is event-driven (Iran, crude, a stronger dollar) rather than belief-driven in the way Soros means it. Reflexivity needs the market’s own perception to be the thing driving the fundamentals — not an oil tanker stuck in the Strait of Hormuz. Right now, Indian equities are mostly reacting to crude prices and FII flows that have very little to do with what Indian retail investors think about the Indian economy.
But the infrastructure for reflexivity to kick in — the wealth effect, the scale of retail participation, a government that has already publicly worried about this exact channel — is now firmly in place.
Which means these corrections might not stay confined to the market.
And it also means that 7.7% growth number isn’t as reassuring as it sounds. It tells you where the economy was in the quarter that just ended. It says nothing about whether traders and mutual fund investors, watching their portfolios shrink right now, will spend the same way in the quarter ahead.
So here’s the real question worth sitting with: has the stock market grown large enough, and tied to enough households, that the barometer can occasionally cause the storm?
